**定义**

**大多数 AI 项目都遵循一个可识别的 pattern: "感知的进度" 跟 "实际的进度" 不匹配**。**这个 pattern 有三个阶段**: **早期高点 (demo 阶段), 团队快速产出令人印象深刻的东西, 动量感觉很好**; **中段低谷 (eval 阶段), 系统化测试浮出 demo 没浮出的失败模式, 动量停滞**; **后期爬坡 (production 阶段), 团队磨过边缘情况、集成、加固, 到达一个真正能交付的东西**。**事先识别这条 S 曲线, 防止团队和客户在低谷恐慌、在 demo 高点宣告胜利**。

**为何在交付中重要**

**Demo 高点危险, 因为它产出过度自信**。**团队感觉有产出, 客户被打动, 有按 demo 轨迹承诺时间线的诱惑**。**这几乎总是错的**。**Demo 阶段在前 20% 的时间里达到 60 到 80% 的感知进度**。**剩下 80% 的时间产出最后 20% 的感知进度, 但那是对 production 重要的部分**。

**Eval 低谷以相反方式危险**。**团队感觉卡住, 客户怀疑项目是否在失败, 有放弃严格测试、回到 demo 般进度的诱惑**。**这也错**。**低谷是项目实际在做最重要工作的地方**: **浮出 "如果不处理就会造成 production 失败" 的失败模式**。**事先命名低谷, 让所有人都预期它, 是 PM 能做的最有用的事之一**。

**运作原理**

**S 曲线有三个阶段, 每个有特征信号和特征风险**。

| 阶段 | 时长 | 感知进度 | 实际进度 | 关键风险 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Demo 高点 | 项目前 20 到 30% | 快 | 真实但狭窄 | 过度承诺、过早宣告胜利、把 demo 误当 production |
| Eval 低谷 | 中段 30 到 50% | 停滞或回退 | 最有价值 | 恐慌、放弃 evals、为了恢复动量换范围 |
| Production 爬坡 | 末段 30 到 50% | 慢但稳定 | 收敛 | 时间压力造成偷工、疲劳、漏掉边缘情况 |

**曲线不对称**。**Demo 高点短而陡**。**低谷长而不适**。**Production 爬坡是日历时间上最长的阶段, 但显示最可靠的进度**。

**Demo 高点详解**

**Demo 高点发生, 因为 LLM 在精挑细选的例子上意外地擅长产出令人印象深刻的输出**。**第一个 prompt, 应用到手挑的输入上, 经常产出让房间安静下来的东西**。**这是真实能力, 不是魔法, 但它是一个狭窄的能力**。**同样的 prompt 应用到真实输入的随机样本上, 在 30 到 50% 上以精挑 demo 没显示的方式失败**。

**团队在这个阶段的工作是享受动量但不承诺它**。**用 demo 跟 stakeholder 建立信心, 同时私下追踪更广的分布**。**内部相信 demo 代表最终产品的团队, 在 eval 低谷到来时会深度失望**。**把 demo 识别为更广分布上一个好点的团队, 是被准备好的**。

**Eval 低谷详解**

**低谷在团队对一份有代表性的测试集 (12.2 的 eval set) 跑第一次系统化评估时开始**。**分数几乎总是比 demo 暗示的低**。**团队意外, 客户有时担忧, 诱惑是要么解释掉它、要么用不同方式重来**。

**两个都不对**。**对的动作是认真对待 eval 结果, 识别失败的类别, 系统化地工作过它们**。**这是磨人的工作**。**每个失败类别通常需要一个具体干预**: **prompt 调整、检索改进、额外上下文、拒绝处理、输出格式**。**每个干预产出一个小的增量改善, 经常是 eval 分数上的 2 到 5 个百分点**。**多个干预在几周里累积**。

**这个阶段, 团队的 status 更新感觉单调**。**"我们在工作过 eval 失败, 当前通过率 78%, 上周 72"**。**工作是真实的但用叙事形式不令人印象深刻**。**PM 的工作是让团队保持信心 (这项工作就是重要的工作), 让客户保持耐心**。

**低谷在 12 到 16 周的项目上典型持续 3 到 6 周**。**它是整个项目里最长的、可见进度缓慢的持续期**。**之前没经历过这个的团队有时会结论说项目在失败**。**事先命名低谷, 并显示渐进的 eval 改善, 防止这个**。

**Production 爬坡详解**

**爬坡在 eval 分数稳定在团队和客户同意可生产的水平时开始**。**工作从 "改善模型" 转到 "加固模型周围的系统"**: **集成、监控、错误处理、用户界面、部署、文档、培训**。**这是一般良好理解的工程工作, 但花时间**。

**爬坡危险, 因为它看起来项目几乎完成**。**模型工作了, demo 印象深刻, eval 分数在目标上**。**Stakeholder 可能推动更早上线**。**PM 的工作是在爬坡阶段维持纪律**, **确保不光鲜的 production 加固工作发生**, 因为**跳过它产出比等待贵得多的 production 失败**。

**把 S 曲线沟通给客户**

**S 曲线应该在第 1 或 2 周被引入给客户, 作为设定预期的一部分**。**措辞是**: **"这是我们预期看到的典型轨迹。早期进度看起来快。中段进度感觉慢, 因为我们在做防止 production 失败的系统化测试。后期进度会稳定但不会每周产出可见 demo, 因为我们在为 production 加固"**。

**大多数客户, 事先看到这条曲线时, 接受它**。**大多数客户, 在第 8 周对进度恐慌后第一次看到时, 觉得更难接受**。**这场对话在第 1 周容易得多**。

**一个有用产物**: **一张简单的图, 显示 S 曲线, 标记项目每个阶段预期的周数**。**每周用实际进度更新**。**团队和客户都能看到项目在哪、应该在哪**。

**PM 决策点**

- 我**有没有在第 1 或 2 周向客户命名 S 曲线**, 在 **demo 高点产出过度自信之前**?
- Demo 高点期间, 我**有没有私下追踪更广的表现**, 而不只是 demo 亮点?
- Eval 低谷期间, 我**有没有让团队和客户保持信心**, **慢工作就是对的工作**?

**注意事项**

- **看起来太好的 demo 可疑**。**如果第一次尝试在精挑例子上产出 95% 质量的输出, 真实输入上的分布几乎肯定更差**。**庆祝之前调查**。
- **低谷期间, 抵抗 "因为进度慢就换方式" 的诱惑**。**低谷应该慢**。**换方式重启低谷而不是结束它**。
- **有些客户想在 demo 高点末尾上线**。**这个代价是损害关系的 production 失败, 比更长的建造更损害**。

**要点总结: AI 项目遵循感知进度的 S 曲线: demo 高点、eval 低谷、production 爬坡。低谷是真正工作发生的地方, 即使感觉卡住。第 1 周向客户命名曲线, 跟着感知进度追踪真实进度, 三个阶段都维持纪律。**

**Qantas 案例**

设想你启动一个 Qantas AI 项目, **给企业销售团队建一个内部助手**, **帮他们为大企业客户起草定制提案**。**团队有活力, 运营 sponsor engaged, 前两周产出一个 striking demo**。**一家大型矿业公司的真实 RFP 被喂进助手**。**助手产出一份提案草稿, 早期迹象显示质量非常高**。**房间被打动**。**运营 sponsor 想知道下周能否给 executive sponsor 看**。

**PM 之前见过这个 pattern, 做两个动作**。**Demo 用合适的措辞给 executive sponsor 看**: **"这是一个高质量的单一例子, 我们预期质量在更广的输入范围上更可变, 下一阶段会告诉我们实际分布长什么样"**。**Executive sponsor 欣赏直接, 没被过度承诺**。

**平行地, 团队开始从过去两年的企业销售 RFP 构建一份更广的 eval set**。**Eval set 有 80 份 RFP, 复杂度、行业、交易规模、客户成熟度各异**。**团队跑当前 prompt 对所有 80 份, 根据跟企业销售运营团队商定的标准给输出打分**。

**结果令人警醒**。**通过率 64%**。**Demo 的 RFP 原来是较容易的之一**。**陌生行业的 RFP、非标准格式的、需要具体技术承诺的产出明显更差的输出**。**团队短暂沮丧**。**运营 sponsor 想知道 demo 是不是误导**。

**这是 eval 低谷的开始**。**PM 让团队保持聚焦**。**每个失败类别被识别**: **矿业和能源的行业特定术语造成术语错误、含非标准定价结构的 RFP 没被处理、需要具体合规承诺的 RFP 漏了它们、非常长的 RFP 让模型丢上下文**。**每个类别得到具体干预**。**每个干预产出 2 到 4 个百分点的 eval 分数改善**。

**接下来四周, 通过率从 64% 爬到 72、76、81**。**团队的每周更新单调, 但趋势稳定**。**运营 sponsor 知道第 1 周引入的那张图, 能看到项目在预期的低谷里、正在爬出来**。**她引用曲线在 executive sponsor 面前维持信心**。

**第 10 周, eval 分数到 86%, 团队和运营 sponsor 同意这对 production 可接受, 附加条件是低置信输出路由到人工 review**。**Production 爬坡开始**。**接下来四周的工作是跟企业销售工作流的集成、培训销售团队怎么用工具、构建人工 review 移交、创建展示团队怎么用工具的 dashboard**。

**第 14 周按时上线**。**企业销售团队使用工具**。**质量跟 eval 分数一致, 人工 review 抓住低置信案例**。**关系加深**。

**有意思的对照是另一个没有事先命名曲线的 Qantas AI 项目**。**那个项目也在第 3 周有 striking demo、第 5 周有清醒的 eval 结果**, **那个项目的 executive sponsor (没被告知要预期低谷) 恐慌, 命令团队 "立刻让它跟 demo 一样好"**。**团队慌乱, 严格评估工作被削减, 团队聚焦在不代表更广分布的看起来印象深刻的 demo 上**。**系统在第 12 周以 "精挑例子上好看、真实案例 35% 失败" 的状态上线**。**上线被回滚**。**项目恢复花了六周, executive sponsor 对团队失去信心**。**这些都不会发生, 如果曲线被事先命名**。

AI 交付的启示: **S 曲线真实、可预测、有后果**。**第 1 周向客户命名它是一个有不成比例效果的小干预**。**这么做的团队保护自己不受 demo 高点的过度自信和 eval 低谷的恐慌**。**不这么做的团队, 在被意外恶化的条件下打两场仗**。

items.title_en: Five delivery health signals to track weekly, beyond burn down
items.title_zh: 每周要追踪的五个交付健康信号 (不是 burn down)
items.body_en:
**Definition**

Traditional project management tracks delivery health through burn down charts: how many tasks remain, how many hours of work, how the trend compares to the plan. In AI projects this is necessary but insufficient. AI projects can have a clean burn down while heading toward production failure, because the burn down measures activity, not outcome. A more useful approach is to track five specific health signals weekly, each of which surfaces a different category of risk that burn down misses.

**Why it matters in delivery**

The most expensive failures in AI delivery are not from running out of time, but from running through the time and arriving at something that does not work in production. A team can complete every planned task on time and still ship a system that fails users. Burn down would have shown green throughout. The five signals described here are designed to catch the kinds of problems that burn down does not see: quality drift, scope reality, dependency stalls, team confidence, and stakeholder alignment.

Each signal is a leading indicator, meaning it changes before the underlying problem becomes visible in conventional metrics. Tracking them weekly gives the team and operating sponsor early warning of issues that would otherwise surface late, when the cost to fix them is high.

**How it works**

The five signals are listed below, with what to measure, what changes mean, and what action to take when a signal is bad.

| Signal | What to measure | Good looks like | Bad looks like | Action when bad |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Eval trend | Pass rate on the agreed eval set, week over week | Steady upward trend, even if slow | Flat, declining, or volatile | Diagnose the category of failure, target the work |
| Scope reality | Number of items in scope, deferred, and in the parking lot | Stable or modest growth in parking lot | Rapid growth in scope, or churn between in scope and deferred | Convene a scope review, prune deliberately |
| Dependency status | Status of the top 3 to 5 external dependencies | All in progress or resolved | One or more blocked, with no movement | Escalate the specific dependency to the named owner |
| Team confidence | Subjective rating from each team member, 1 to 5 | Most at 3 or 4, no 1s sustained | Multiple 1s or 2s, or a downward trend | Investigate cause, address root issue not symptom |
| Stakeholder alignment | Whether sponsor and key stakeholders agree on status, scope, and next steps | Aligned, with documented agreement | Sponsor says one thing, stakeholders behave differently | Surface the misalignment, schedule a joint meeting |

Each signal can be captured in 10 minutes weekly. Together they take less than an hour. The leverage is high.

**The eval trend signal**

The eval trend is the most important single signal. It is the direct measure of whether the actual product is improving. The right way to track it: a single chart, updated weekly, showing eval score over time. Annotate the chart with major changes (model version, prompt iteration, eval set expansion) so trends can be interpreted.

A healthy eval trend climbs steadily, even if slowly. A flat trend means the team is busy but not improving. A declining trend usually means the eval set has been expanded faster than the model has been improved. A volatile trend means the team is making changes without controlling for what is being changed.

What is not useful: tracking eval score as a single number without trend, comparing to a target without showing trajectory, or only reporting the score in the steering committee where it is too late to act.

**The scope reality signal**

Scope reality tracks whether the project's scope is stable. Items in scope (will be delivered), deferred (v2 or v1.5), and in the parking lot (under discussion). The healthy state is roughly stable: a few items move between categories each week, mostly as items are decided.

What is unhealthy: rapid expansion of scope (signs of scope creep not being managed), rapid growth in the parking lot (signs the team is collecting ideas without resolving them), or items oscillating between in scope and deferred (signs of unresolved disagreement).

What to do when scope reality goes bad depends on the pattern. Rapid expansion calls for a scope review with the sponsor. Parking lot growth calls for a review session to either promote or retire items. Oscillation calls for surfacing the underlying disagreement.

**The dependency status signal**

The risk register (from 14.5) lists external dependencies. This signal asks: are the top dependencies moving? Each top dependency has an owner, an expected resolution date, and a current status. The signal is good if all are progressing. The signal is bad if one or more have been at the same status for two or more weeks.

Stalled dependencies are particularly dangerous because they are invisible. The team is doing other work, the dependency is "pending", and weeks pass before anyone notices. The weekly check forces attention on dependency status, which is half the work of resolving them.

**The team confidence signal**

Team confidence is a subjective measure but a valuable one. Each team member rates their confidence in the project on a 1 to 5 scale, weekly, in a short async survey or a one minute check at the standup. The numbers themselves matter less than the trend. A team that was at 4 last week and is at 2 this week is signalling something the PM needs to investigate.

The signal does not always reveal what the issue is. A drop in team confidence might be about technical concerns, about a difficult stakeholder, about a personal issue affecting one team member, or about something the team senses but cannot articulate. The PM's job when this signal goes bad is to investigate, not to optimise for higher numbers. Trying to make the number look good without addressing the underlying issue is one of the worst mistakes a PM can make.

**The stakeholder alignment signal**

Stakeholder alignment is whether the sponsor and the team's understanding of project status, scope, and next steps matches what other stakeholders believe. It is checked by listening: in the weekly check-in with the operating sponsor, does the sponsor describe the project the same way the team does? In conversations with users or blockers during the week, do they describe the project the same way?

When stakeholders describe the project differently, alignment has slipped. The team is still moving, but in a direction not all stakeholders endorse. This signal often goes bad before any other signal, and it catches issues that the others miss.

**Putting the five together**

The five signals do not produce a single number. They are a dashboard. In the weekly check-in with the operating sponsor, the PM walks through each, with the current state and any change from last week. Most weeks, most signals are good. When a signal goes bad, the conversation focuses there. When multiple signals go bad in the same week, the project is in genuine trouble and the conversation goes to the engagement partner.

**PM decision points**

- Have I set up the five signals at project start, or am I only tracking task completion?
- Am I capturing the signals weekly, or are they aspirational?
- When a signal goes bad, do I act on the cause, or do I optimise the metric?

**Watch outs**

- Do not let any single signal dominate. The eval trend is the most direct measure of product quality, but a project with a great eval trend and collapsing team confidence is in trouble.
- Subjective signals (team confidence, stakeholder alignment) require trust. If team members feel their honest answers will be punished, the numbers become useless.
- Reporting the signals to the steering committee can be useful but risky. The committee may try to manage the metrics rather than the underlying reality. Filter for the committee, but keep the full set internal.

**Takeaway: track five weekly delivery health signals beyond burn down: eval trend, scope reality, dependency status, team confidence, stakeholder alignment. Each is a leading indicator. Each takes minutes to capture. Together they surface the categories of failure that burn down misses.**

**Qantas story**

Imagine running a Qantas AI project, an internal tool for the customer experience team that classifies and routes incoming customer complaints. The project is 14 weeks. The team is six people. The PM sets up the five signals in week one.

Each Friday, the PM spends 30 minutes updating the dashboard. The eval trend is taken from the latest automated eval run. Scope reality is the count of items in scope, deferred, and in the parking lot, from the project's shared document. Dependency status is read from the risk register. Team confidence comes from a short Friday morning survey with one question. Stakeholder alignment is the PM's subjective rating based on the week's conversations.

The dashboard is shared with the operating sponsor in the weekly check-in. The conversation each week is short: the PM walks through the five signals in five minutes, the sponsor asks questions, decisions are made on anything that has gone bad.

In week three, the eval trend signal goes bad: the score has dropped from 71 percent to 67 percent. The team had expanded the eval set the previous week and the new examples were harder than the original set. The signal triggered investigation. The drop was real but expected, given the eval set expansion. The team and sponsor agree this is a healthy correction, and the team continues. Without the signal, the drop might have been missed or, worse, misinterpreted as regression.

In week six, the team confidence signal goes bad: two team members rate confidence at 2, one at 1. The PM investigates. The cause is not technical: the team is exhausted from a difficult workshop the previous week with a particularly aggressive operating team member. The PM addresses this directly with the operating sponsor, the workshop format is adjusted, and the next workshop is much smoother. Team confidence recovers within two weeks. Without the signal, the issue might have festered for another month and produced burnout.

In week nine, the stakeholder alignment signal goes bad: in conversation with a senior customer service manager, the manager describes the project as "automating complaint responses", whereas the team and sponsor have been describing it as "classifying and routing complaints to the right human responder". The misalignment is significant: one is about replacing humans, the other is about helping them. The PM raises this in the next steering committee, the misalignment is surfaced, and the sponsor takes responsibility for re-aligning the customer service leadership. Without the signal, this misalignment would have surfaced at launch, when the customer service team realised the system was not what they thought.

In week 12, the dependency status signal goes bad: the integration dependency on the CRM system has been at the same status for three weeks. The PM escalates the named owner directly. The owner has been struggling with competing priorities. With escalation through the engagement partner, the dependency is moved to the front of the queue and resolved in week 13. Without the signal, the dependency might have slipped past launch.

The launch in week 14 goes smoothly. None of the issues that arose during the project caused launch delay or production failure, because each one was caught by one of the signals while it was still cheap to fix.

The interesting comparison is with a different Qantas project that tracked only burn down. The burn down showed green throughout. The launch was delayed by eight weeks because of issues that the five signals would have caught: dependency stall not noticed until late, stakeholder misalignment not surfaced until launch readiness, team confidence drop not addressed until burnout was visible.

The lesson for AI delivery is that activity is not the right thing to measure. Outcome is. The five signals are different views of outcome: is the product getting better, is the scope under control, are the dependencies moving, is the team healthy, are the stakeholders aligned. Each takes minutes to track. Together they protect against the failure modes that burn down does not see.
items.body_zh:
**定义**

**传统项目管理通过 burn down 图追踪交付健康**: **还剩多少任务、多少工时、趋势怎么跟计划比**。**AI 项目里这个必要但不够**。**AI 项目可以有干净的 burn down 同时朝 production 失败前进**, 因为 **burn down 衡量活动, 不是结果**。**更有用的方式是每周追踪五个具体的健康信号**, **每个浮出 burn down 错过的不同类别风险**。

**为何在交付中重要**

**AI 交付里最贵的失败不是来自时间耗尽, 而是来自时间耗完后到达一个在生产里不工作的东西**。**一个团队能按时完成每一个计划任务, 还交付一个对用户失败的系统**。**Burn down 全程会显示绿色**。**这里描述的五个信号被设计来抓 burn down 看不到的问题**: **质量漂移、范围现实、依赖停滞、团队信心、stakeholder 对齐**。

**每个信号是先行指标, 意思是它在底层问题在常规指标里变得可见之前就变化**。**每周追踪它们, 给团队和运营 sponsor 早期警告 issue**, **不然这些 issue 会晚浮出, 那时候修它们的成本高**。

**运作原理**

**下面列出五个信号, 带 "测什么、变化什么意思、信号差时采取什么行动"**。

| 信号 | 测什么 | 好看起来像 | 差看起来像 | 差时的行动 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Eval 趋势 | 商定 eval set 上的通过率, 周对周 | 稳定上升趋势, 即使慢 | 平、下降、或波动 | 诊断失败类别, 靶向工作 |
| 范围现实 | 范围内、推迟、parking lot 的项数 | 稳定或 parking lot 适度增长 | 范围快速增长, 或范围内和推迟之间的搅动 | 召集范围 review, 刻意修剪 |
| 依赖状态 | 前 3 到 5 个外部依赖的状态 | 全部进行中或解决 | 一个或多个被阻塞, 没动作 | 把具体依赖升级到具名 owner |
| 团队信心 | 每个团队成员的主观评分, 1 到 5 | 大多数 3 或 4, 没有持续的 1 | 多个 1 或 2, 或下降趋势 | 调查原因, 处理根问题不是症状 |
| Stakeholder 对齐 | Sponsor 和关键 stakeholder 是否同意 status、scope、下一步 | 对齐, 带文档化协议 | Sponsor 说一回事, stakeholder 行为不同 | 浮出错位, 安排联合会议 |

**每个信号每周 10 分钟能捕捉**。**合起来用不到一小时**。**杠杆高**。

**Eval 趋势信号**

**Eval 趋势是最重要的单一信号**。**它是 "实际产品是否在改善" 的直接衡量**。**追踪的对的方式**: **一张图, 每周更新, 显示 eval 分数随时间**。**用主要变化标注图 (模型版本、prompt 迭代、eval set 扩大), 这样趋势能被解读**。

**健康的 eval 趋势稳定上升, 即使慢**。**平的趋势意思是团队忙但没在改善**。**下降趋势通常意味着 eval set 被扩大得比模型被改善得快**。**波动趋势意思是团队在改东西但没控制改了什么**。

**什么没用**: **把 eval 分数当一个数追踪、没显示轨迹就跟目标比较、只在 steering committee 报分数 (太晚没法行动)**。

**范围现实信号**

**范围现实追踪项目范围是否稳定**。**范围内的项 (会交付)、推迟的 (v2 或 v1.5)、parking lot 里的 (在讨论中)**。**健康状态是大致稳定**: **每周几项在类别之间移动, 大多是因为项被决定**。

**不健康**: **范围快速扩张 (没在管 scope creep 的迹象)、parking lot 快速增长 (团队在收集想法不解决它们)、项在 "范围内" 和 "推迟" 之间摇摆 (未解决分歧的迹象)**。

**范围现实变差时做什么取决于 pattern**。**快速扩张需要跟 sponsor 的范围 review**。**Parking lot 增长需要 review 会议来提升或退役项**。**摇摆需要浮出底层分歧**。

**依赖状态信号**

**风险登记表 (来自 14.5) 列外部依赖**。**这个信号问**: **前几个依赖在动吗?** **每个前依赖有 owner、预期解决日期、当前状态**。**信号好, 如果都在推进**。**信号差, 如果一个或多个保持同样状态两周以上**。

**停滞的依赖特别危险**, 因为**它们不可见**。**团队在做其他工作, 依赖 "pending", 几周过去没人注意**。**每周检查强制注意依赖状态, 这是解决它们一半的工作**。

**团队信心信号**

**团队信心是主观衡量但有价值**。**每个团队成员对项目的信心打 1 到 5 分, 每周, 在一个短的异步调查或 standup 上一分钟检查里**。**数字本身没比趋势重要**。**上周 4、这周 2 的团队在发信号, PM 需要调查**。

**信号不总揭示 issue 是什么**。**团队信心下降可能是关于技术关切、难搞 stakeholder、影响一位团队成员的个人 issue、或团队感知到但说不出来的东西**。**这个信号变差时 PM 的工作是调查, 不是优化更高数字**。**试图让数字看好但不处理底层 issue, 是 PM 能犯的最糟错误之一**。

**Stakeholder 对齐信号**

**Stakeholder 对齐是 sponsor 和团队对项目 status、scope、下一步的理解是否匹配其他 stakeholder 相信的**。**通过倾听检查**: **跟运营 sponsor 的每周 check-in 里, sponsor 描述项目的方式跟团队一样吗?** **本周跟用户或阻断者的对话里, 他们描述项目的方式一样吗?**

**当 stakeholder 不同地描述项目, 对齐滑了**。**团队还在动, 但朝一个不是所有 stakeholder 都认可的方向**。**这个信号经常在任何其他信号之前变差, 它抓住其他错过的 issue**。

**把五个合起来**

**五个信号不产出单一数字**。**它们是 dashboard**。**跟运营 sponsor 的每周 check-in 里, PM 走过每一个, 带当前状态和上周以来的任何变化**。**大多数周, 大多数信号都好**。**信号变差时, 对话聚焦那里**。**当同一周多个信号变差, 项目真的有麻烦, 对话上升到 engagement partner**。

**PM 决策点**

- 我**有没有在项目开始时设置五个信号**, 还是**只在追踪任务完成**?
- 我**有没有每周捕捉信号**, 还是**它们是愿望**?
- 信号变差时, 我**对原因行动**, 还是**优化指标**?

**注意事项**

- **不要让任何单一信号支配**。**Eval 趋势是产品质量的最直接衡量, 但有好 eval 趋势同时团队信心崩溃的项目, 在麻烦中**。
- **主观信号 (团队信心、stakeholder 对齐) 需要信任**。**如果团队成员觉得诚实答案会被惩罚, 数字变得无用**。
- **把信号汇报给 steering committee 可能有用但有风险**。**委员会可能尝试管理指标而不是底层现实**。**为委员会过滤, 但保持完整集合内部**。

**要点总结: 追踪 burn down 之外的五个每周交付健康信号: eval 趋势、范围现实、依赖状态、团队信心、stakeholder 对齐。每个是先行指标。每个花几分钟捕捉。合起来浮出 burn down 错过的失败类别。**

**Qantas 案例**

设想你跑一个 Qantas AI 项目, **给客户体验团队的内部工具, 分类和路由进来的客户投诉**。**项目 14 周**。**团队六人**。**PM 第 1 周设置五个信号**。

**每个周五, PM 花 30 分钟更新 dashboard**。**Eval 趋势从最新自动 eval 跑取**。**范围现实是从项目共享文档来的 "范围内、推迟、parking lot" 的项数**。**依赖状态从风险登记表读**。**团队信心来自周五早晨带一个问题的短调查**。**Stakeholder 对齐是 PM 基于本周对话的主观评分**。

**Dashboard 在每周 check-in 跟运营 sponsor 共享**。**每周对话短**: **PM 五分钟走过五个信号, sponsor 问问题, 对任何变差的做决定**。

**第 3 周, eval 趋势信号变差**: **分数从 71% 降到 67%**。**团队上周扩大了 eval set, 新例子比原集合难**。**信号触发调查**。**降是真的但预期的, 鉴于 eval set 扩大**。**团队和 sponsor 同意这是健康的修正, 团队继续**。**没有信号, 降可能被错过, 或更糟, 被误解为回退**。

**第 6 周, 团队信心信号变差**: **两位团队成员评信心 2, 一位 1**。**PM 调查**。**原因不是技术的**: **团队从上周跟一位特别 aggressive 的运营团队成员的难搞 workshop 里精疲力尽**。**PM 直接跟运营 sponsor 处理这个, workshop 格式被调整, 下次 workshop 顺得多**。**团队信心两周内恢复**。**没有信号, issue 可能再发酵一个月, 产出 burnout**。

**第 9 周, stakeholder 对齐信号变差**: **跟一位资深客服经理的对话里, 经理描述项目为 "自动化投诉回应", 而团队和 sponsor 一直描述它为 "把投诉分类和路由到对的人工回应者"**。**错位显著**: **一个是关于替代人, 另一个是关于帮他们**。**PM 在下次 steering committee 提出, 错位被浮出, sponsor 承担责任重新对齐客服领导层**。**没有信号, 这个错位会在上线时浮出**, **当客服团队意识到系统不是他们以为的**。

**第 12 周, 依赖状态信号变差**: **对 CRM 系统的集成依赖保持同一状态三周**。**PM 直接升级具名 owner**。**Owner 一直在跟竞争性优先级搏斗**。**通过 engagement partner 升级, 依赖被移到队伍前面, 第 13 周解决**。**没有信号, 依赖可能滑过上线**。

**第 14 周上线顺利**。**项目期间出现的任何 issue 都没造成上线延迟或 production 失败**, 因为**每个都被信号之一抓住, 在修它还便宜的时候**。

**有意思的对照是只追踪 burn down 的另一个 Qantas 项目**。**Burn down 全程显示绿**。**上线被推迟八周, 因为五个信号会抓住的 issue**: **依赖停滞晚才被注意、stakeholder 错位上线 readiness 才浮出、团队信心降在 burnout 可见之前没被处理**。

AI 交付的启示: **活动不是对的衡量东西**。**结果是**。**五个信号是结果的不同视图**: **产品在变好吗、范围在控制下吗、依赖在动吗、团队健康吗、stakeholder 对齐吗**。**每个花几分钟追踪**。**合起来防止 burn down 看不到的失败模式**。

items.title_en: Doing the right thing vs doing the thing right, and which failure is more dangerous
items.title_zh: 做对的事 vs 把事做对, 哪个出问题更危险
items.body_en:
**Definition**

Two failure modes are common in AI delivery, and they require different responses. The first is "doing the wrong thing well", where the team executes flawlessly on a project that should not have been done, or on a use case that does not serve the actual user need. The second is "doing the right thing poorly", where the team is on the correct project but is executing badly. The two failures look similar in status reports (the project is in trouble) but require completely different interventions. This item is about telling them apart and knowing which is more dangerous.

**Why it matters in delivery**

In conventional consulting wisdom, doing the wrong thing well is the more dangerous failure: it produces a polished solution to an irrelevant problem, which is expensive and hard to recover from. In AI delivery this remains true, but the diagnostic is harder because the symptoms of both failures overlap. A project that is failing on execution looks similar to a project that is succeeding on execution but solving the wrong problem.

The deeper reason this distinction matters: the response to each failure is opposite. If the team is doing the wrong thing well, the response is to pause, re-examine the use case, and potentially re-direct. If the team is doing the right thing poorly, the response is to keep going, improve execution, and not change the project. Doing the wrong response to either failure makes it worse. Pausing a project that just needs execution improvement creates churn. Pushing harder on a project that is on the wrong thing produces a polished mistake.

**How it works**

The diagnostic distinguishes between the two failures through five questions.

| Question | Doing the wrong thing well | Doing the right thing poorly |
|---|---|---|
| Are users excited when they see early outputs? | No, even though outputs are polished | Yes, but outputs need refinement |
| Is the eval set itself reasonable? | No, the eval set tests for wrong things | Yes, the eval set is right but pass rate is low |
| Does the operating team find the system useful in practice? | No, even when it works as specified | Yes when it works, frustrated when it does not |
| Would killing the project produce relief or panic? | Relief, possibly hidden | Panic, the work matters |
| Is the team's energy about "let us improve" or "let us do something different"? | Different | Improve |

If two or more answers point to "doing the wrong thing well", the project needs a re-examination. If two or more point to "doing the right thing poorly", the project needs execution improvement, not re-direction.

**Symptoms that look like one but are the other**

The diagnostic is hard because both failures can present similarly. A few patterns where the surface symptom misleads.

*Eval scores are low.* Could be either. If the eval set is testing the right things and pass rate is low, the project is executing poorly on the right thing. If the eval set is testing things the operating team does not care about, the project is doing the wrong thing well (the team is improving its score on irrelevant tests).

*Users are unenthusiastic.* Could be either. If users like the idea but the early outputs are rough, the project is on the right thing but executing poorly. If users have stopped engaging, are not coming to working sessions, or describe the project flatly when asked, the project may be on the wrong thing.

*Project feels slow.* Could be either. If the team feels slow but engaged, focused on real problems, this is the eval valley of a right-thing project. If the team feels slow and increasingly disengaged, doing work that does not feel meaningful, this may be a wrong-thing project.

The PM's job is to look past the surface symptom and ask the diagnostic questions deliberately.

**Which is more dangerous**

The standard answer is "doing the wrong thing well", and that remains true in AI delivery. The reasons:

A wrong-thing project that is well executed will ship. It will then be used briefly, found unhelpful, and abandoned. The team is left with a polished artifact that does not produce business value. The cost is the entire project budget. The cost of recognising the wrong-thing in week six and pivoting is much smaller than completing it.

A right-thing project that is poorly executed will produce visible struggles. The team and client will see them. The interventions to improve execution are well understood: more engineering effort, better evals, more workshops with users, more time. The cost of poor execution is recoverable if recognised. The cost of the wrong thing is harder to recover.

The second reason: a wrong-thing project damages relationships. The operating team that participated in a wrong-thing project, and saw it launched, often becomes skeptical of future AI projects. The opportunity cost of the wrong thing is not just this project's budget, but the harder time the next project will have getting cooperation.

**Communicating the diagnosis**

When the diagnosis is "doing the right thing poorly", the conversation with the client is easier. The team owns the execution gap, names specific improvements, and asks for time or resources. Clients accept this when it is presented honestly.

When the diagnosis is "doing the wrong thing well", the conversation is harder. The team is essentially saying "we have built this well, and we do not think it solves the right problem". The framing matters. It is not "we wasted your money", it is "what we have learned by building has shown us the use case needs to be reshaped". The reshaping can often save most of the work that has been done.

The conversation is best had in private with the operating sponsor first, before any wider stakeholder. The sponsor needs to be part of the diagnosis, not surprised by it. From there, the conversation broadens to the steering committee with a recommendation, not a problem.

**PM decision points**

- For each project I am running, can I name with confidence whether the team is doing the right thing or the wrong thing?
- Am I asking the diagnostic questions deliberately, or only when something seems wrong?
- When I diagnose wrong-thing, am I willing to surface it to the operating sponsor honestly?

**Watch outs**

- The team will resist a wrong-thing diagnosis, because it implies the work so far has limited value. The PM has to be willing to make the diagnosis even when the team disagrees.
- The operating sponsor sometimes wants to keep going on a wrong-thing project to avoid the political cost of changing direction. The PM's job is to make the costs of continuing visible.
- Sometimes the diagnosis is partial: a project is doing the right thing on some dimensions and the wrong thing on others. In that case, the response is to keep the right parts and re-direct the wrong parts.

**Takeaway: doing the wrong thing well and doing the right thing poorly look similar in symptoms but require opposite responses. Five diagnostic questions distinguish them. Wrong-thing failures are more dangerous because they produce polished mistakes and damage future AI projects. The harder conversation is the more valuable one to have.**

**Qantas story**

Imagine running a Qantas AI project to build a customer service chat tool for the airport ground operations team. The tool is designed to help duty managers respond to customer enquiries during operational disruptions. By week eight, the project is in trouble. The eval scores are at 78 percent and not climbing. The team is working hard. The operating sponsor is concerned. The instinct in week eight is to push for better execution: more eval cycles, more prompt iteration, more model experimentation.

The PM, instead, runs the diagnostic.

Are users excited when they see early outputs? Mixed. The duty managers who have seen demos appreciate the technical capability but have not asked to use it themselves. They have not pulled the team into their workflows. When asked directly, several say "this is impressive but I do not think it fits how I actually work during a disruption".

Is the eval set itself reasonable? The eval set was constructed by the team with the operating sponsor's input. The duty managers were not closely involved. When the team reviews the eval set with three actual duty managers, the duty managers describe many of the eval inputs as "unrealistic" or "not the kind of question I would type into a tool during a disruption".

Does the operating team find the system useful in practice? When the team places the early version in front of duty managers during a simulated disruption exercise, the duty managers use it once, find it slower than their existing process, and stop using it for the rest of the exercise.

Would killing the project produce relief or panic? In a private conversation with the operating sponsor, the PM asks the question directly. The sponsor pauses, then admits that killing the project would produce relief, mixed with concern about how to explain it.

Is the team's energy about "let us improve" or "let us do something different"? The team is increasingly raising the question of whether the use case is right. One team member, in a recent retrospective, said directly that "we are building something well but I do not think they will use it".

Four out of five answers point to "doing the wrong thing well". The project is executing competently but on a use case that does not match how duty managers actually work during disruptions. Pushing harder on execution would produce a polished tool that would not be used.

The PM raises this with the operating sponsor in a private one-on-one. The framing is not "we have wasted your money", it is "what we have learned by building has shown us the use case needs to be reshaped". The sponsor, given the diagnostic, agrees.

The team and sponsor go back to the duty managers with a different question: "during a disruption, what is the hardest 30 seconds of your work, where AI could genuinely help?" The conversations reveal a different use case: the duty managers do not want a chat tool, they want a system that automatically generates the first draft of the customer notification template based on the disruption parameters, which they can then edit. This is faster than typing and faster than searching for the template they used last time.

The project is re-scoped in week nine. Three weeks of work are repurposed: the prompt engineering, the eval infrastructure, and the duty manager relationships all transfer. The new use case is built in seven weeks instead of the eight weeks remaining, because the team is now solving a problem the duty managers actually have. The launched tool is enthusiastically adopted.

The interesting counterfactual is what would have happened if the diagnostic had not been run. The team would have spent the remaining six weeks improving the chat tool, the launch would have been on schedule, the duty managers would have used it briefly and abandoned it, and the project would have been classified as a failure six months later. The work would have been good, but on the wrong thing.

The lesson for AI delivery is that "doing the right thing" is not a given. It needs to be tested explicitly, especially when other signals suggest something is off. The diagnostic is uncomfortable because it sometimes recommends pivoting. The cost of pivoting in week eight is much less than the cost of completing the wrong thing in week 14. The PM who is willing to ask the harder question saves more value than the PM who optimises execution on a project that should not have been continued.
items.body_zh:
**定义**

**AI 交付里两种失败模式常见, 需要不同回应**。**第一是 "做错的事但做得好"**, **团队在一个不该做的项目上、或在一个不服务实际用户需求的 use case 上, 执行得完美**。**第二是 "做对的事但做得差"**, **团队在对的项目上, 但执行得差**。**两种失败在 status 报告里看起来相似 (项目在麻烦中), 但需要完全不同的干预**。**这一节是关于区分它们, 以及知道哪个更危险**。

**为何在交付中重要**

**传统咨询智慧里, 做错的事但做得好是更危险的失败**: **它产出对无关问题的精致解决方案, 贵且难恢复**。**AI 交付里这仍然真, 但诊断更难**, 因为**两种失败的症状重叠**。**一个在执行上失败的项目, 看起来跟一个在执行上成功但解决错问题的项目相似**。

**这种区分重要的更深原因**: **对每种失败的回应是相反的**。**如果团队在做错的事但做得好, 回应是暂停、重审 use case、可能重新定向**。**如果团队在做对的事但做得差, 回应是继续、改善执行、不改项目**。**对任一失败做错的回应让它更糟**。**暂停一个只需要改善执行的项目制造搅动**。**对一个做错事情的项目更加用力, 产出精致的错误**。

**运作原理**

**诊断通过五个问题区分两种失败**。

| 问题 | 做错的事但做得好 | 做对的事但做得差 |
|---|---|---|
| 用户看到早期输出时兴奋吗? | 不, 即使输出精致 | 是, 但输出需要精炼 |
| eval set 本身合理吗? | 不, eval set 测错的东西 | 是, eval set 对但通过率低 |
| 运营团队在实际中觉得系统有用吗? | 不, 即使它按规格工作 | 工作时是, 不工作时挫败 |
| 杀掉项目会产出宽慰还是恐慌? | 宽慰, 可能隐藏 | 恐慌, 工作有意义 |
| 团队的能量是关于 "我们改善" 还是 "我们换" 的? | 换 | 改善 |

**如果两个或更多答案指向 "做错的事但做得好", 项目需要重审**。**如果两个或更多指向 "做对的事但做得差", 项目需要改善执行, 不是重新定向**。

**看起来像一种但实际是另一种的症状**

**诊断难, 因为两种失败能呈现得相似**。**几个表面症状误导的 pattern**。

*Eval 分数低*。**可能是任一种**。**如果 eval set 测对的东西、通过率低, 项目在对的事上执行得差**。**如果 eval set 测运营团队不在意的东西, 项目在做错的事但做得好 (团队在改善无关测试上的分数)**。

*用户不热情*。**可能是任一种**。**如果用户喜欢主意但早期输出粗糙, 项目在对的事上但执行得差**。**如果用户停止 engage、不来工作会议、被问时平淡描述项目, 项目可能在错的事上**。

*项目感觉慢*。**可能是任一种**。**如果团队感觉慢但 engaged, 聚焦在真问题上, 这是对的事项目的 eval 低谷**。**如果团队感觉慢且越来越 disengaged, 做的工作感觉没意义, 这可能是错的事项目**。

**PM 的工作是看穿表面症状, 刻意问诊断问题**。

**哪个更危险**

**标准答案是 "做错的事但做得好"**, **这在 AI 交付里仍然真**。**原因**:

**一个做错的事但执行得好的项目会上线**。**然后被短暂使用、发现没用、被抛弃**。**团队留下一个不产出业务价值的精致产物**。**成本是整个项目预算**。**第 6 周识别错的事并 pivot 的成本, 比完成它小得多**。

**一个做对的事但执行得差的项目会产出可见的挣扎**。**团队和客户会看到**。**改善执行的干预良好理解**: **更多工程精力、更好的 evals、跟用户更多 workshop、更多时间**。**执行差的成本如果被识别可恢复**。**做错事的成本更难恢复**。

**第二个原因**: **做错的事项目损害关系**。**参与了做错事项目的运营团队, 看到它上线, 经常对未来 AI 项目变得怀疑**。**做错的事的机会成本不只是这个项目的预算, 是下个项目获得合作时会遇到的更难时光**。

**沟通诊断**

**当诊断是 "做对的事但做得差", 跟客户的对话更容易**。**团队拥有执行缺口, 命名具体改善, 请求时间或资源**。**客户在它被诚实呈现时接受**。

**当诊断是 "做错的事但做得好", 对话更难**。**团队本质上在说 "我们建得好, 但我们不认为它解决对的问题"**。**措辞重要**。**不是 "我们浪费了你的钱", 是 "我们通过建造学到的东西显示 use case 需要重塑"**。**重塑经常能保留大部分已做的工作**。

**对话最好先私下跟运营 sponsor 进行, 在任何更广 stakeholder 之前**。**Sponsor 需要是诊断的一部分, 不是被它惊吓**。**从那, 对话扩大到 steering committee, 带建议, 不是问题**。

**PM 决策点**

- 对我正在跑的每个项目, 我**能不能有信心地命名团队在做对的事还是错的事**?
- 我**有没有刻意问诊断问题**, 还是**只在事情看起来不对时**?
- 当我诊断 "错的事", 我**愿意诚实地把它浮给运营 sponsor 吗**?

**注意事项**

- **团队会抵抗错的事诊断**, 因为**它暗示到目前为止的工作价值有限**。**PM 必须愿意做诊断, 即使团队不同意**。
- **运营 sponsor 有时想继续做错的事项目, 以避免改变方向的政治成本**。**PM 的工作是让继续的成本可见**。
- **有时诊断是局部的**: **一个项目在某些维度上做对的事、在另一些维度上做错的事**。**那种情况, 回应是保留对的部分、重新定向错的部分**。

**要点总结: 做错的事但做得好, 和做对的事但做得差, 症状看起来相似, 但需要相反回应。五个诊断问题区分它们。错的事失败更危险, 因为它们产出精致错误、损害未来 AI 项目。更难的对话是更值得有的。**

**Qantas 案例**

设想你跑一个 Qantas AI 项目, **给机场地面运营团队建一个客服聊天工具**。**工具被设计来帮值班经理在运营中断期间回应客户咨询**。**到第 8 周, 项目在麻烦中**。**Eval 分数在 78%, 不在爬**。**团队在努力工作**。**运营 sponsor 担心**。**第 8 周的本能是推动更好的执行**: **更多 eval 循环、更多 prompt 迭代、更多模型实验**。

**PM 反而跑诊断**。

**用户看到早期输出时兴奋吗?** **混合**。**看过 demo 的值班经理欣赏技术能力, 但没要求自己用**。**他们没把团队拉进他们的工作流**。**被直接问时, 几位说 "这印象深刻, 但我不觉得它适合我在中断期间实际怎么工作"**。

**eval set 本身合理吗?** **eval set 由团队带着运营 sponsor 输入构建**。**值班经理没紧密参与**。**当团队跟三位实际值班经理 review eval set, 值班经理描述很多 eval 输入为 "不现实" 或 "不是我在中断期间会输入工具的那种问题"**。

**运营团队在实际中觉得系统有用吗?** **当团队在模拟中断演习中把早期版本放在值班经理面前, 值班经理用了一次, 发现比他们现有流程慢, 演习剩下时间停止用**。

**杀掉项目会产出宽慰还是恐慌?** **跟运营 sponsor 的私下对话里, PM 直接问问题**。**Sponsor 停顿, 然后承认杀掉项目会产出宽慰, 混合着关于怎么解释的关切**。

**团队的能量是关于 "我们改善" 还是 "我们换" 的?** **团队越来越提出 use case 是否对的问题**。**一位团队成员在最近的回顾里直接说 "我们在建一个好东西, 但我不觉得他们会用"**。

**五个答案里四个指向 "做错的事但做得好"**。**项目在执行得能干, 但在不匹配值班经理在中断期间实际怎么工作的 use case 上**。**在执行上更用力会产出一个精致但不会被用的工具**。

**PM 在私下一对一里跟运营 sponsor 提出这个**。**措辞不是 "我们浪费了你的钱", 是 "我们通过建造学到的东西显示 use case 需要重塑"**。**Sponsor, 给定诊断, 同意**。

**团队和 sponsor 带不同问题回到值班经理面前**: **"中断期间, 你工作中最难的 30 秒是什么, AI 能真正帮上忙的?"** **对话揭示一个不同的 use case**: **值班经理不想要聊天工具, 他们想要一个根据中断参数自动生成客户通知模板的第一稿的系统, 然后他们能编辑**。**这比打字快, 也比搜索上次用的模板快**。

**项目第 9 周被重新 scope**。**三周工作被重新利用**: **prompt 工程、eval 基础设施、值班经理关系都转移**。**新 use case 在七周内建成, 而不是剩下的八周**, 因为**团队现在在解决值班经理实际有的问题**。**上线的工具被热情采纳**。

**有意思的反事实是没跑诊断会发生什么**。**团队会花剩下的六周改善聊天工具, 上线按时, 值班经理短暂使用并抛弃, 项目六个月后被分类为失败**。**工作会是好的, 但在错的事上**。

AI 交付的启示: **"做对的事" 不是给定的**。**它需要被明确测试, 尤其当其他信号暗示什么不对时**。**诊断不舒服, 因为它有时建议 pivot**。**第 8 周 pivot 的成本比第 14 周完成错的事的成本小得多**。**愿意问更难问题的 PM, 比在不该继续的项目上优化执行的 PM, 节省更多价值**。

items.title_en: Team morale as a leading indicator: what to listen for, what to watch for
items.title_zh: 团队士气作为先行指标: 听什么、看什么
items.body_en:
**Definition**

Team morale is the collective emotional and psychological state of the delivery team: their confidence in the project, their satisfaction with the work, their trust in each other and in the PM. In AI delivery, team morale is a leading indicator of project trouble: when morale drops, the underlying causes have usually been present for two to three weeks before the morale change shows up, and they will produce visible project problems two to three weeks later if not addressed. Reading morale accurately, and acting on it before it manifests in deliverables, is one of the most valuable skills a PM can develop.

**Why it matters in delivery**

A common PM failure is to treat morale as a softer concern, a "nice to track" alongside the hard metrics of progress and quality. This view is mistaken. Morale is a hard predictor of delivery outcomes. A team with sustained low morale produces worse work, makes more mistakes, has higher turnover, and damages client relationships. A team with sustained high morale produces better work, finds creative solutions, and weathers setbacks more gracefully.

The deeper reason morale matters as a leading indicator: morale responds to problems before the problems become visible in deliverables. A team that senses misalignment with the client, before any concrete misalignment has occurred, will show drops in morale weeks before the misalignment manifests. A team that is being asked to compromise on quality, before any specific compromise has been made, will show signs of frustration that precede any visible quality issue. PMs who learn to read morale accurately get an early warning system for problems they would otherwise see late.

**How it works**

Morale is read through three channels: what people say, what people do, and what people do not say or do.

**What people say**

The verbal signals are the easiest to read but also the easiest to misinterpret. A few specific patterns to listen for.

| Verbal signal | What it usually means |
|---|---|
| Frequent use of "we" and "our project" | Engagement and ownership |
| Shift to "they want us to" and "the client said" | Engagement dropping, team feeling instrumental |
| Specific frustrations about a person | Could be real, could be displacement of a deeper issue |
| Generalised complaints about the project | Often a sign of deeper concerns the person cannot yet articulate |
| Silence in meetings where they used to speak | Strong signal that engagement has dropped |
| Sarcasm about the project or client | Late stage signal, often indicates frustration that has been suppressed |

The patterns matter more than isolated statements. One frustrated comment from one team member in one meeting is normal. A pattern of similar comments from multiple team members over multiple meetings is a signal.

**What people do**

Behavioural signals are often more reliable than verbal ones, because people who are unhappy often try to say the right things while their behaviour reveals the truth.

| Behavioural signal | What it usually means |
|---|---|
| Attendance at optional sessions drops | Engagement is dropping |
| Slack messages become shorter and less frequent | Disengagement starting |
| Code review comments become perfunctory | The work has become a chore |
| People stop volunteering for stretch tasks | Confidence in the project is dropping |
| Lateness or absence increases | Active disengagement, often the late stage |
| Side conversations and back channels emerge | The team is processing something they cannot raise officially |

Behavioural signals are particularly valuable because they are involuntary. A team member who is frustrated can choose to say the right things in a meeting, but they cannot choose to feel enthusiastic about volunteering for the next workshop.

**What people do not say or do**

The third channel is the absence of things that would normally be present. This is the hardest to read, but often the most informative.

| Absence signal | What it usually means |
|---|---|
| Nobody is excited about a milestone that should be exciting | The team has internalised that the milestone does not really matter |
| No questions during a stakeholder meeting that should have generated them | Team has stopped engaging or has lost the agency to ask |
| Nobody volunteers to do the post-meeting follow up | Energy for the project has dropped |
| The team's lunch conversations are no longer about the work | Mental detachment has begun |
| No one disagrees with the PM in working sessions | Either the PM is always right (unlikely) or the team has stopped pushing back |

The absence of disagreement is particularly important. A team that never pushes back is not a team that agrees, it is a team that has given up. This is a late stage morale signal that requires immediate intervention.

**Causes of morale issues**

Morale drops have identifiable causes, almost always in one of four categories.

| Category | Examples | Typical fix |
|---|---|---|
| Sense of futility | Working on something the team does not believe will be used | Surface the doubt, run the diagnostic from 16.3 |
| Relational tension | Conflict with a stakeholder, friction within the team | Address the specific relationship issue |
| Workload imbalance | Some team members overloaded, others underused | Rebalance workload, often through honest conversation |
| Lack of recognition | The team's work is not being seen or appreciated | Make the work visible to senior stakeholders |

The PM's job, when morale drops, is to investigate which category is in play and address the cause. Trying to boost morale generically (more team lunches, more pizza, more compliments) without addressing the cause is performative and often makes things worse, because it signals that the PM does not understand what is really happening.

**How to track morale without it being awkward**

A few practical methods that work.

*Weekly one minute check ins.* Each team member rates their confidence and energy on a 1 to 5 scale. Async, in a shared channel. Takes one minute per person per week. The numbers themselves are not the goal, the trend is.

*Monthly retrospectives.* 30 minutes, structured around what is going well and what could be better. The PM listens more than talks. The retrospective surfaces issues that did not surface in standups.

*Quiet one to ones.* Once every two to three weeks, a 15 minute one to one with each team member. Not a status review, an open conversation. The question that works: "what is one thing about the project you would change if you could?".

The combination of these three captures most of the morale signal. None of them are heavy. All of them require the PM to actually pay attention and respond, not just collect data.

**PM decision points**

- Am I tracking morale deliberately, or am I assuming it is fine because nobody has complained?
- When morale drops, am I investigating the cause, or am I optimising the metric?
- Am I creating space for team members to raise concerns without consequence, or are they likely to suppress concerns?

**Watch outs**

- Morale is not the same as energy. A team can be tired and have good morale, or rested and have low morale. The signal is about engagement and confidence, not about how late people are working.
- Some PMs over-index on morale and avoid hard conversations because they fear damaging morale. This is backwards. The hard conversation, done well, usually improves morale because it shows the PM is willing to address real issues.
- Morale among the delivery team is one signal. Morale among the client's operating team is another, distinct signal. Both matter. Do not assume one tells you about the other.

**Takeaway: team morale is a leading indicator of project health. Read it through what people say, what they do, and what is absent. When morale drops, investigate the cause in one of four categories: futility, relational tension, workload, recognition. Address the cause, do not optimise the metric. The morale signal arrives weeks before the deliverable signal, which is what makes it valuable.**

**Qantas story**

Imagine running a Qantas AI project, an internal knowledge tool for the customer service team. The project is 16 weeks. The team is seven people: a PM, a tech lead, three engineers, a data analyst, and a designer. The project starts well, with high morale across the team.

In week six, the PM notices a subtle change. The tech lead, who usually pushes back actively on prompt design decisions, has been quieter in the last two working sessions. The PM does not raise it publicly but pays attention.

In week seven, two more signals appear. One of the engineers misses the optional Friday wrap up that he has attended every week since project start. The designer's code review comments have become shorter and less detailed. Individually, each could be coincidence. Together, they are a pattern.

The PM schedules quiet one to ones with the tech lead, the engineer, and the designer over the next ten days. Each conversation is open, not a status review. The PM asks what they would change about the project if they could.

The tech lead reveals something the PM had not seen. The operating sponsor has been making decisions in the steering committee that contradict decisions the team had made in working sessions. The tech lead feels his technical recommendations are not being respected. He has stopped pushing back because he does not see the point.

The engineer reveals something different. He had volunteered for a stretch task in week four that he had been excited about, but a scope change in week five had absorbed his time into less interesting work. He felt his enthusiasm had been used for marketing the project, then redirected to grunt work. He had not raised it because he did not want to seem like he was complaining.

The designer reveals a third issue. Her code review comments had become perfunctory because she felt the prompts were being changed faster than she could thoughtfully review them, and her thoughtful comments were being ignored.

Three different causes. The tech lead is experiencing a relational issue with the sponsor. The engineer is experiencing workload mis-allocation and lack of recognition. The designer is experiencing futility about her review work.

The PM addresses each. With the tech lead, the PM has a direct conversation with the operating sponsor about the pattern of steering committee decisions contradicting team decisions, and a process is agreed where major decisions are jointly discussed before being made. With the engineer, the PM rebalances the work, returning some of the interesting stretch task to him and shifting the grunt work elsewhere. With the designer, the PM slows the prompt iteration cycle and ensures her comments are responded to specifically.

Over the next three weeks, the morale signals reverse. The tech lead pushes back actively again. The engineer volunteers for the next stretch task. The designer's code review comments become detailed and substantive. The team is healthy again, in time for the production climb of weeks 10 to 14.

The interesting comparison is with another Qantas AI project where the PM did not pay attention to morale signals. The same kinds of issues built up unaddressed. By week 10, two team members had quietly applied for transfers to other teams. By week 12, the project was delivering but with significant quality issues that the disengaged team was no longer catching. The launch was delayed by four weeks because of late-discovered defects.

The lesson for AI delivery is that morale is not soft, it is hard. It predicts project outcomes weeks ahead of any other signal. Reading it accurately requires attention to what people say, what they do, and what is absent. Acting on it requires identifying the cause and addressing it, not optimising the metric. The PM who develops this skill protects both the team and the project, and produces better outcomes than the PM who treats morale as something to track but not act on.
items.body_zh:
**定义**

**团队士气是交付团队的集体情绪和心理状态**: **他们对项目的信心、对工作的满意、对彼此和 PM 的信任**。**AI 交付里, 团队士气是项目麻烦的先行指标**: **当士气下降, 底层原因通常在士气变化显现之前已经存在两到三周, 如果不处理, 它们会在两到三周后产出可见的项目问题**。**准确读士气、在它显现在交付物里之前行动, 是 PM 能发展的最有价值的技能之一**。

**为何在交付中重要**

**PM 的常见失败是把士气当作较软的关切, 跟进度和质量的硬指标并列的 "可以追踪"**。**这种观点错**。**士气是交付结果的硬预测器**。**持续低士气的团队产出更差的工作、犯更多错误、有更高流失、损害客户关系**。**持续高士气的团队产出更好的工作、找到创造性解决方案、更优雅地承受挫折**。

**士气作为先行指标重要的更深原因**: **士气在问题在交付物里变得可见之前对问题做出反应**。**一个感知到跟客户错位的团队, 在任何具体错位发生之前, 会在错位显现前几周显示士气下降**。**一个被要求在质量上妥协的团队, 在任何具体妥协被做出之前, 会显示挫败迹象, 在任何可见的质量问题之前**。**学会准确读士气的 PM, 得到一个对 "他们本来会晚看到的问题" 的早期预警系统**。

**运作原理**

**士气通过三个渠道读**: **人们说什么、人们做什么、人们不说不做什么**。

**人们说什么**

**语言信号最容易读但也最容易误读**。**几个具体 pattern 要听**。

| 语言信号 | 通常意味着什么 |
|---|---|
| 频繁使用 "我们" 和 "我们的项目" | Engagement 和拥有感 |
| 转向 "他们想让我们" 和 "客户说" | Engagement 在降, 团队感觉工具化 |
| 关于一个人的具体挫败 | 可能真实, 可能是更深 issue 的转移 |
| 关于项目的概括性抱怨 | 经常是这个人还无法清楚表达的更深关切的迹象 |
| 在他们以前发言的会议里沉默 | engagement 降下来的强信号 |
| 关于项目或客户的讽刺 | 晚期信号, 经常表明被压抑的挫败 |

**Pattern 比孤立的陈述更重要**。**一位团队成员在一次会议里的一句挫败评论是正常的**。**多位团队成员在多次会议里的相似评论 pattern 是信号**。

**人们做什么**

**行为信号经常比语言信号更可靠**, 因为**不开心的人经常试图说对的话, 而他们的行为揭示真相**。

| 行为信号 | 通常意味着什么 |
|---|---|
| 出席可选 session 减少 | engagement 在降 |
| Slack 消息变短和更不频繁 | disengagement 开始 |
| Code review 评论变得敷衍 | 工作变成苦工 |
| 人们停止志愿做拉伸任务 | 对项目的信心在降 |
| 迟到或缺席增加 | 主动 disengagement, 经常是晚期 |
| 出现旁支对话和后渠道 | 团队在处理他们无法正式提出的东西 |

**行为信号特别有价值, 因为它们是不自主的**。**一位挫败的团队成员能选择在会议里说对的话, 但他们不能选择对下一次 workshop 感到热情**。

**人们不说不做什么**

**第三个渠道是 "通常会在场的东西的缺席"**。**这最难读, 但经常最具信息量**。

| 缺席信号 | 通常意味着什么 |
|---|---|
| 没人对应该激动的里程碑激动 | 团队内化了 "这个里程碑实际上不重要" |
| Stakeholder 会议本应产生的问题没人问 | 团队停止 engage 或失去了问的能动性 |
| 没人志愿做会后跟进 | 项目的能量下降了 |
| 团队的午餐对话不再关于工作 | 心智脱离开始 |
| 工作会议里没人跟 PM 不同意 | 要么 PM 总是对 (不太可能), 要么团队停止 push back |

**没有不同意特别重要**。**一个从不 push back 的团队不是同意的团队, 是放弃的团队**。**这是需要立即干预的晚期士气信号**。

**士气问题的原因**

**士气下降有可识别的原因, 几乎总在四个类别之一**。

| 类别 | 例子 | 典型修复 |
|---|---|---|
| 无意义感 | 在团队不相信会被使用的东西上工作 | 浮出怀疑, 跑 16.3 的诊断 |
| 关系紧张 | 跟 stakeholder 冲突、团队内摩擦 | 处理具体关系 issue |
| 工作量不均 | 一些团队成员过载, 另一些用不足 | 重新平衡工作量, 经常通过诚实对话 |
| 缺乏认可 | 团队的工作没被看到或欣赏 | 让工作对资深 stakeholder 可见 |

**PM 的工作, 当士气下降时, 是调查哪个类别在场, 并处理原因**。**通用地提升士气 (更多团队午餐、更多披萨、更多赞美) 而不处理原因, 是表演性的, 经常让事情更糟**, 因为**它发信号说 PM 不理解实际发生什么**。

**怎么追踪士气, 不让它尴尬**

**几个奏效的实际方法**。

*每周一分钟 check-in*。**每位团队成员把信心和能量打 1 到 5 分**。**异步, 在共享渠道**。**每人每周一分钟**。**数字本身不是目标, 趋势是**。

*每月回顾*。**30 分钟, 围绕 "什么在跑通、什么能更好" 结构化**。**PM 听多于说**。**回顾浮出 standup 里没浮出的 issue**。

*安静的一对一*。**每两到三周一次, 跟每位团队成员 15 分钟一对一**。**不是 status review, 是开放对话**。**奏效的问题**: **"项目里有一件事如果你能改你会改什么?"**

**这三者的组合捕捉大部分士气信号**。**没一个是重的**。**全部要求 PM 真的关注和回应, 不只是收集数据**。

**PM 决策点**

- 我**有没有刻意追踪士气**, 还是**假设它 fine 因为没人抱怨**?
- 当士气下降, 我**调查原因**, 还是**优化指标**?
- 我**有没有创造空间让团队成员提出关切而无后果**, 还是**他们可能压抑关切**?

**注意事项**

- **士气跟能量不一样**。**一个团队能累且有好士气, 或休息好但低士气**。**信号是关于 engagement 和信心, 不是关于人们工作得多晚**。
- **有些 PM 过度看重士气, 避免难对话因为怕损害士气**。**这反了**。**做得好的难对话, 通常改善士气**, 因为**它显示 PM 愿意处理真 issue**。
- **交付团队的士气是一个信号**。**客户运营团队的士气是另一个、不同的信号**。**两个都重要**。**不要假设一个告诉你另一个**。

**要点总结: 团队士气是项目健康的先行指标。通过人们说什么、做什么、缺席什么来读它。当士气下降, 在四个类别之一调查原因: 无意义、关系紧张、工作量、认可。处理原因, 不优化指标。士气信号在交付物信号之前几周到达, 这是它的价值。**

**Qantas 案例**

设想你跑一个 Qantas AI 项目, **给客服团队的内部知识工具**。**项目 16 周**。**团队七人**: **一位 PM、一位技术负责人、三位工程师、一位数据分析师、一位设计师**。**项目开始得好, 团队士气高**。

**第 6 周, PM 注意到一个微妙变化**。**技术负责人, 通常在 prompt 设计决策上主动 push back, 在最近两次工作会议里更安静**。**PM 没公开提, 但关注**。

**第 7 周, 又出现两个信号**。**一位工程师错过了从项目开始每周都参加的可选周五收尾**。**设计师的 code review 评论变短、更不详细**。**单独看, 每个可能是巧合**。**合起来, 是 pattern**。

**PM 接下来十天里安排跟技术负责人、工程师、设计师的安静一对一**。**每场对话开放, 不是 status review**。**PM 问他们如果能改会改项目什么**。

**技术负责人揭示一些 PM 没看到的东西**。**运营 sponsor 在 steering committee 上做的决定, 跟团队在工作会议上做的决定矛盾**。**技术负责人觉得他的技术建议没被尊重**。**他停止 push back 因为他看不到意义**。

**工程师揭示不同的东西**。**他第 4 周志愿了一个他兴奋的拉伸任务, 但第 5 周的范围变化把他的时间吸收到不那么有意思的工作里**。**他觉得他的热情被用来营销项目, 然后被重定向到苦工**。**他没提出来, 因为不想显得像在抱怨**。

**设计师揭示第三个 issue**。**她的 code review 评论变敷衍, 因为她觉得 prompt 被改得比她能深思熟虑 review 快, 她深思熟虑的评论被忽略**。

**三个不同原因**。**技术负责人在经历跟 sponsor 的关系 issue**。**工程师在经历工作量错配和缺乏认可**。**设计师在经历对她 review 工作的无意义感**。

**PM 处理每一个**。**跟技术负责人, PM 跟运营 sponsor 直接对话, 关于 "steering committee 决定矛盾团队决定" 的 pattern, 商定一个流程, 主要决定在做出之前联合讨论**。**跟工程师, PM 重新平衡工作, 把一部分有意思的拉伸任务还给他, 把苦工转到别处**。**跟设计师, PM 减慢 prompt 迭代周期, 确保她的评论被具体回应**。

**接下来三周, 士气信号反转**。**技术负责人再次主动 push back**。**工程师志愿下一个拉伸任务**。**设计师的 code review 评论变得详细和实质**。**团队再次健康, 及时迎接第 10 到 14 周的 production 爬坡**。

**有意思的对照是另一个 PM 没注意士气信号的 Qantas AI 项目**。**同类 issue 不被处理地累积**。**到第 10 周, 两位团队成员悄悄申请了转到其他团队**。**到第 12 周, 项目在交付但有显著质量 issue, disengaged 的团队不再抓到**。**上线被推迟四周, 因为晚发现的缺陷**。

AI 交付的启示: **士气不软, 它硬**。**它在任何其他信号之前几周预测项目结果**。**准确读它需要关注人们说什么、做什么、缺席什么**。**对它行动需要识别原因并处理, 不是优化指标**。**发展这种技能的 PM 保护团队和项目, 产出比 "把士气当作要追踪但不要行动的东西" 的 PM 更好的结果**。

items.title_en: When to stop and redo, and how to explain it to the client
items.title_zh: 何时该停下来重做, 以及怎么向客户解释
items.body_en:
**Definition**

Some AI projects reach a point where the right move is to stop, throw away part of the work, and start that part over. The signals that this point has been reached are recognisable. The decision to act on them is hard, because stopping feels like failure and starting over feels like waste. This item is about recognising the moment when stopping is the right call, communicating the decision honestly to the client, and executing the restart in a way that preserves what is salvageable.

**Why it matters in delivery**

Continuing on a flawed foundation is one of the most expensive mistakes in delivery. The cost of stopping in week six and redoing two weeks of work is small. The cost of continuing on that flawed foundation through to launch, then discovering at week 14 that the system does not actually work, is much larger. Yet the social and psychological pressure to keep going is strong. Stopping feels like admitting failure. Stopping triggers difficult conversations with the client. Stopping might affect the team's reputation. Each pressure pushes the team to continue past the point where stopping would have been right.

The PM's job is to make the stopping decision when the signals warrant it, despite the pressures against it. Doing this well is one of the most senior judgments in AI delivery. It requires being honest about what the team has built, being willing to discard work that is not serving the project, and being skilled at communicating the decision so that it strengthens rather than weakens the client relationship.

**How it works**

Three categories of signal indicate that stopping and redoing may be the right call.

*Foundational error.* The team has built on an assumption that turns out to be wrong. Common examples: the eval set was constructed against criteria the operating team disagrees with, the prompt strategy is fundamentally mismatched to the use case, the data being used is the wrong dataset for the actual problem. When the foundation is wrong, continuing to build on it produces increasingly elaborate wrong outputs.

*Compounding mistakes.* The team has made a series of small decisions, each defensible individually, that together have produced an architecture that does not work. The system is patched, the patches are patched, and the team is spending more time on patches than on substantive work. The system is technically functional but is degenerating.

*Misaligned with what users actually do.* The team has built something that works against the eval set but does not work in real user contexts. This is related to the 16.3 wrong-thing diagnosis, but specifically refers to the case where the team has invested significantly and the misalignment is structural rather than cosmetic.

When one or more of these signals is present, the question is not "should we keep improving the current work" but "should we keep the current work as the basis for further improvement". Sometimes the answer is no.

**The cost of continuing versus the cost of restarting**

Before stopping, the PM should estimate honestly the cost of each path.

*Cost of continuing.* How many weeks until the project would have shipped, and how much of that time would be spent working around the flaw? What would the launched product be like, given the flaw? What would the client and users think of it?

*Cost of restarting.* How much of the existing work can be salvaged? How long would it take to redo the parts that need redoing? What is the impact on timeline, budget, and team energy?

The estimate is rarely precise, but the order of magnitude matters. If continuing costs 6 weeks of frustrating work to ship a flawed product, and restarting costs 4 weeks to ship a better one, restarting is obviously right. If continuing costs 2 weeks and restarting costs 8 weeks, restarting is probably wrong unless the launched product would be unusable.

The honest cost estimate is the work the PM has to do. Most teams underestimate the cost of continuing on a flawed foundation, because the cost is hidden in many small struggles that compound. Most teams overestimate the cost of restarting, because they psychologically count work already done as sunk cost they do not want to abandon.

**How to communicate the decision to the client**

The conversation has three parts.

*Part 1: Frame the discovery, not the failure.* The conversation opens with what the team has learned, not with what is wrong. "Through the work over the past four weeks, we have discovered something important about how this needs to be built." This framing makes the conversation forward-looking rather than apologetic.

*Part 2: Present the choice as a recommendation, not a problem.* The team comes to the client with a recommendation, not with a request for the client to decide. "We recommend stopping the current build and restarting with a different approach. Here is why, here is what we would do differently, here is what it would cost in time and budget." This is professional. Bringing the client a problem to solve is amateur.

*Part 3: Be specific about what is being kept and what is being discarded.* A blanket "we are starting over" is alarming. A specific "we are keeping the eval set, the operating team relationships, the infrastructure, and the integration plan, and redoing the prompt strategy and the data pipeline" is reassuring. It also forces the team to be honest about what is genuinely salvageable.

The framing that works: this is a normal part of AI delivery. The first version of any AI system is often not the right version. The team that recognises this and restarts at the right time delivers better outcomes than the team that pushes through. The client almost always accepts this when it is presented confidently.

**Internal team management during a restart**

Restarts are hard on team morale. People have invested in the work being discarded. The PM's job is to manage the emotional response while ensuring the restart happens cleanly.

A few specific practices.

*Acknowledge the discarded work, do not pretend it had no value.* The team learned things by doing the discarded work. Those learnings inform the restart. Name them explicitly.

*Make the restart fast and decisive.* A drawn out restart, where the team is half discarding and half preserving, is worse than a clean restart. Within two weeks of the decision, the team should be working on the new approach with the discarded work archived.

*Use the restart to address other latent issues.* The team often knows of related issues that have been festering. The restart is an opportunity to address them too. Ask the team what they would change while everything is being reconsidered.

*Reset stakeholder expectations honestly.* Some stakeholders were excited about the discarded work. They need to be told what is happening, why, and what to expect now. The PM owns these conversations, not the team.

**PM decision points**

- Am I willing to recommend stopping when the signals warrant it, or am I psychologically committed to continuing?
- Have I estimated the cost of continuing honestly, including the hidden costs of working around the flaw?
- When I bring the recommendation to the client, am I bringing it as a recommendation or as a problem?

**Watch outs**

- Stopping should not be the first response to a difficult phase. Most projects go through difficult phases without needing to restart. Reserve the stopping recommendation for genuine foundational issues, not for normal valley conditions (see 16.1).
- The team will resist a restart proposal at first. They have invested in the work. The PM has to be willing to make the case even against initial team resistance.
- After the restart decision is made, do not litigate it again. If the team keeps relitigating, the restart will be slow and partial. Make the decision, communicate it, and execute.

**Takeaway: some AI projects need to stop and restart parts of the work. The signals are foundational error, compounding mistakes, and misalignment with users. Estimate the cost of each path honestly. Communicate the decision to the client as a recommendation, framed as discovery. Manage the team through the restart with acknowledgment, decisiveness, and honest reset of expectations.**

**Qantas story**

Imagine running a Qantas AI project to build an internal tool for the cargo customer service team: a system that drafts responses to shipping enquiries by drawing on past correspondence and current shipping rates. By week six, the project is producing outputs that the team is privately uncomfortable with. The eval scores look acceptable (around 75 percent), but in real testing with cargo customer service agents, the drafts are routinely being rewritten substantially before being sent. The agents are polite about the tool, but in their own words, "it is faster to write from scratch than to fix what it produces".

The PM runs the 16.3 diagnostic and concludes the project is not quite in the wrong-thing category, but there is a foundational issue. The team had constructed the system around generating polished, complete responses, on the theory that a polished draft would save agent time. The reality is that cargo customer service is highly contextual: each customer has a relationship history, each shipping situation has specifics, and a polished generic response is harder to adapt than a structured outline. The agents do not want polished prose, they want structured input that they can quickly fill in.

This is a foundational error. Continuing to improve the polished prose generator would produce a tool that the agents would not use. Restarting with a structured outline generator would produce a tool that fits the agents' actual workflow.

The PM estimates the cost honestly. Continuing the current approach: probably four more weeks of prompt engineering to push the eval score from 75 to 85 percent, followed by an unenthusiastic launch and probable abandonment within three months. Restarting: probably three weeks to redo the prompt strategy and output format, while keeping the eval set, the data integration, the agent relationships, and the infrastructure. The cost comparison is clear: restarting is faster than continuing, and produces a tool that actually gets used.

The PM brings this to the operating sponsor. The framing is the three part structure described above. "Through the work over the past six weeks, we have learned something important about how cargo customer service works. We recommend changing our approach. Here is what we are keeping, here is what we are redoing, here is what it costs."

The operating sponsor's response is initially defensive. She had advocated for the polished prose approach internally and feels personally invested. The PM is patient. The framing is repeated: this is not a failure, this is a discovery. The work to date has produced learnings that make the new approach possible. The operating sponsor, given time to think, agrees with the recommendation.

The communication to the executive sponsor happens in the next steering committee, with the operating sponsor leading and the PM supporting. The message is the same: we have learned something important and we are adjusting accordingly. The executive sponsor accepts the recommendation and asks for an updated timeline.

The team is told the next day. The reaction is mixed. The tech lead, who had been growing uncomfortable with the prompt complexity required to produce polished prose, is relieved. Two engineers, who had invested heavily in the prompt design, are initially disappointed. The PM acknowledges the discarded work explicitly: the eval set is staying, the data pipeline is staying, the agent feedback patterns are informing the new approach. The discarded work is not wasted, it has produced the understanding that makes the new approach right.

The restart happens in 16 days. The new structured outline generator is built and tested with the same eval set, achieves similar eval scores, and produces outputs that the agents actively want to use. The launch happens in week 13, one week ahead of the original schedule. The agents use the tool consistently after launch.

The interesting comparison is with what might have happened without the stop. The team would have spent four more weeks improving prompts to produce more polished prose, launched a tool that the agents found cumbersome, and watched usage drop within a month of launch. The project would have been classified as a marginal failure six months later.

The lesson for AI delivery is that the willingness to stop and restart, when the signals warrant it, is one of the most senior skills in this work. It requires being honest about what is not working, willing to discard work that is not serving the project, and skilled at communicating the decision. Done well, a stop-and-restart strengthens the client relationship rather than weakening it, because the client sees a team that values getting the right outcome over preserving the appearance of progress. That is a deeply valuable reputation to build.
items.body_zh:
**定义**

**有些 AI 项目到达一个点, 对的动作是停下、扔掉部分工作、把那部分重做**。**到达这个点的信号可识别**。**对它行动的决定难**, 因为**停下感觉像失败, 重做感觉像浪费**。**这一节是关于识别 "停下是对的选择" 的时刻、诚实地把决定沟通给客户、以保留可挽救东西的方式执行重做**。

**为何在交付中重要**

**在有缺陷的基础上继续是交付里最贵的错误之一**。**第 6 周停下并重做两周工作的成本小**。**在那个有缺陷的基础上继续到上线, 然后第 14 周发现系统实际上不工作的成本大得多**。**但 "继续" 的社交和心理压力强**。**停下感觉像承认失败**。**停下触发跟客户的难对话**。**停下可能影响团队声誉**。**每种压力推动团队继续, 经过 "停下本应是对的" 的点**。

**PM 的工作是在信号支持时做出停下决定, 尽管有反对的压力**。**做好这件事是 AI 交付里最资深的判断之一**。**它需要诚实地看团队建了什么、愿意丢弃不服务项目的工作、擅长沟通决定, 让它加强而不是削弱客户关系**。

**运作原理**

**三类信号表明停下和重做可能是对的选择**。

*基础错误*。**团队建在一个事实证明错的假设上**。**常见例子**: **eval set 被对照运营团队不同意的标准构建、prompt 策略跟 use case 基本不匹配、被用的数据是实际问题的错数据集**。**当基础错, 在它上面继续建产出越来越精致的错输出**。

*累积的错误*。**团队做了一系列小决定, 每个单独看可辩护, 合起来产出了一个不工作的架构**。**系统打补丁, 补丁打补丁, 团队在补丁上花的时间多于在实质工作上**。**系统技术上工作, 但在退化**。

*跟用户实际做的事错位*。**团队建了在 eval set 上工作、但在真实用户上下文里不工作的东西**。**这跟 16.3 的错事诊断相关, 但具体指 "团队已经显著投资, 错位是结构性的而不是化妆性的"**。

**当一个或多个信号在场, 问题不是 "我们应该继续改善当前工作", 而是 "我们应该把当前工作作为进一步改善的基础"**。**有时候答案是不**。

**继续的成本 vs 重做的成本**

**在停下之前, PM 应该诚实估计每条路径的成本**。

*继续的成本*。**项目要几周才上线, 那段时间多少花在绕过缺陷上?** **鉴于缺陷, 上线的产品会怎样?** **客户和用户会怎么看待它?**

*重做的成本*。**多少现有工作能被挽救?** **重做需要重做的部分要多久?** **对时间线、预算、团队能量的影响是什么?**

**估计很少精确, 但数量级重要**。**如果继续花 6 周令人挫败的工作上线一个有缺陷产品, 重做花 4 周上线一个更好的, 重做明显对**。**如果继续花 2 周、重做花 8 周, 重做可能错, 除非上线产品不可用**。

**诚实的成本估计是 PM 要做的工作**。**大多数团队低估在有缺陷基础上继续的成本**, 因为**成本藏在累积的许多小挣扎里**。**大多数团队高估重做的成本**, 因为**他们心理上把已做的工作当作他们不想抛弃的沉没成本**。

**怎么跟客户沟通决定**

**对话有三部分**。

*第一部分: 把它框架成发现, 不是失败*。**对话开始于团队学到了什么, 不是什么错了**。**"通过过去四周的工作, 我们发现了关于这个怎么需要被建的重要东西"**。**这种措辞让对话向前看而不是道歉**。

*第二部分: 把选择呈现为建议, 不是问题*。**团队带着建议来找客户, 不是带着请求让客户决定**。**"我们建议停下当前建造、用不同方式重做。这是为什么、这是我们会不同地做什么、这是时间和预算成本"**。**这是专业的**。**带客户一个要解决的问题是业余的**。

*第三部分: 关于保留什么、丢弃什么要具体*。**一句笼统的 "我们重新开始" 令人警觉**。**具体的 "我们保留 eval set、运营团队关系、基础设施、集成计划, 重做 prompt 策略和数据管道" 令人安心**。**它也强迫团队对什么真的可挽救诚实**。

**奏效的措辞**: **这是 AI 交付的正常一部分**。**任何 AI 系统的第一版经常不是对的版**。**识别这个并在对的时间重做的团队, 比硬推过去的团队交付出更好的结果**。**客户在它被自信呈现时几乎总是接受**。

**重做期间的内部团队管理**

**重做对团队士气难**。**人们在被丢弃的工作上投资过**。**PM 的工作是管理情绪反应, 同时确保重做干净发生**。

**几个具体实践**。

*承认被丢弃的工作, 不要假装它没价值*。**团队通过做被丢弃的工作学到了东西**。**那些学习告知重做**。**明确命名它们**。

*让重做快速而决定性*。**拖延的重做, 团队一半丢弃一半保留, 比干净的重做更糟**。**决定后两周内, 团队应该在新方式上工作, 被丢弃的工作归档**。

*用重做处理其他潜在 issue*。**团队经常知道相关在发酵的 issue**。**重做是处理它们的机会**。**问团队他们会改什么, 当一切都在被重新考虑时**。

*诚实重置 stakeholder 预期*。**有些 stakeholder 对被丢弃的工作激动**。**他们需要被告知发生什么、为什么、现在期待什么**。**PM 拥有这些对话, 不是团队**。

**PM 决策点**

- 我**愿意在信号支持时建议停下吗**, 还是**心理上承诺继续**?
- 我**有没有诚实估计继续的成本**, 包括 **绕过缺陷的隐藏成本**?
- 当我把建议带给客户, 我**带的是建议还是问题**?

**注意事项**

- **停下不应该是对难阶段的第一反应**。**大多数项目度过难阶段不需要重做**。**把停下建议留给真正的基础 issue, 不是正常低谷条件 (见 16.1)**。
- **团队一开始会抵抗重做提议**。**他们在工作里投资过**。**PM 必须愿意做案子, 即使对抗最初的团队抵抗**。
- **重做决定做出后, 不要再次诉讼它**。**如果团队不停地再次诉讼, 重做会慢和局部**。**做决定、沟通、执行**。

**要点总结: 有些 AI 项目需要停下和重做部分工作。信号是基础错误、累积错误、跟用户错位。诚实估计每条路径的成本。把决定作为建议沟通给客户, 框架成发现。带着承认、决定性、诚实重置预期管理团队度过重做。**

**Qantas 案例**

设想你跑一个 Qantas AI 项目, **给货运客服团队建一个内部工具**: **一个系统通过引用过往通信和当前运费起草对运输咨询的回应**。**到第 6 周, 项目在产出团队私下不舒服的输出**。**Eval 分数看起来可接受 (大约 75%), 但跟货运客服坐席的真实测试里, 草稿经常在发送前被显著重写**。**坐席对工具客气, 但用他们自己的话, "从头写比修它产出的更快"**。

**PM 跑 16.3 诊断, 结论是项目不完全在错事类别, 但有一个基础 issue**。**团队围绕生成精致完整的回应构建了系统, 理论是精致草稿会节省坐席时间**。**现实是货运客服高度上下文相关**: **每个客户有关系历史、每个运输情况有具体细节、一份精致通用回应比结构化大纲难适应**。**坐席不想要精致 prose, 他们想要能快速填的结构化输入**。

**这是基础错误**。**继续改善精致 prose 生成器会产出坐席不会用的工具**。**用结构化大纲生成器重做会产出符合坐席实际工作流的工具**。

**PM 诚实估计成本**。**继续当前方式**: **可能再四周 prompt 工程把 eval 分数从 75% 推到 85%, 然后不热情上线、可能三个月内被抛弃**。**重做**: **可能三周重做 prompt 策略和输出格式, 同时保留 eval set、数据集成、坐席关系、基础设施**。**成本对比清楚**: **重做比继续快, 产出实际被用的工具**。

**PM 把这带给运营 sponsor**。**措辞是上面描述的三部分结构**。**"通过过去六周的工作, 我们学到了关于货运客服怎么工作的重要东西。我们建议改变方式。这是我们保留的、这是我们重做的、这是成本"**。

**运营 sponsor 的反应一开始是防御的**。**她在内部倡导精致 prose 方式, 感觉个人投资**。**PM 耐心**。**措辞被重复**: **这不是失败, 这是发现**。**到目前为止的工作产出了让新方式可能的学习**。**运营 sponsor, 给了时间想, 同意建议**。

**对 executive sponsor 的沟通在下次 steering committee 发生, 运营 sponsor 主讲, PM 支持**。**消息一样**: **我们学到了重要的东西, 我们在相应调整**。**Executive sponsor 接受建议, 要求更新的时间线**。

**团队第二天被告知**。**反应混合**。**技术负责人, 一直对 "产出精致 prose 所需的 prompt 复杂性" 越来越不舒服, 松了口气**。**两位工程师, 在 prompt 设计里投资重, 一开始失望**。**PM 明确承认被丢弃的工作**: **eval set 留着、数据管道留着、坐席反馈 pattern 在告知新方式**。**被丢弃的工作没浪费, 它产出了让新方式对的理解**。

**重做在 16 天里发生**。**新的结构化大纲生成器被建造和测试, 用同样的 eval set, 达到相似的 eval 分数, 产出坐席主动想用的输出**。**上线在第 13 周发生, 比原计划提前一周**。**坐席上线后持续使用工具**。

**有意思的对照是没停下会发生什么**。**团队会再花四周改善 prompt 产出更精致 prose, 上线一个坐席觉得笨重的工具, 看着上线一个月内使用下降**。**项目会在六个月后被分类为边际失败**。

AI 交付的启示: **在信号支持时停下和重做的意愿, 是这一行最资深的技能之一**。**它需要诚实看不工作的东西、愿意丢弃不服务项目的工作、擅长沟通决定**。**做好的停下和重做加强而不是削弱客户关系**, 因为**客户看到一个团队重视 "得到对的结果" 多于 "保持进度的外观"**。**那是一份深度有价值的声誉去建立**。
